lines: A support desk's search tool turns every ticket into a vector every single night, the entire collection, start to finish.
Most of those tickets closed weeks ago and haven't changed a single word since.
And yet the bill for doing this keeps climbing right alongside the size of the collection.
So what one change would actually bring that bill down the most, without putting correctness at risk at all?
Would shrinking the model to something cheaper and a little less accurate do it?
Or is there a way to skip almost all of that nightly work outright, for free.
answer: Swapping in a weaker model trades away quality everywhere, on every single ticket, just to save money.
The better move is noticing that an edit touches one chunk of text, so only that one chunk actually needs redoing.

lines: Here's the mechanism underneath that idea, stated plainly.
Take a fingerprint of each small chunk of text on its own, never the whole document at once, and keep that fingerprint stored alongside its vector.
The next night, compare the fresh fingerprint against the stored one. Match, skip it entirely. Different, redo just that one chunk.
Now, how fast can any of this actually run, and what does running it cost.
A published study states its own method honestly: one fixed length of text per item, the largest batch size its hardware could hold, and a stated rental price for that hardware.
Rerunning that same method on far smaller hardware, and saying so plainly, is reading a study for its approach, not borrowing its headline number and pretending it's yours.
There's a second kind of ceiling worth naming separately, though.

A service reached over the open internet instead of run on your own hardware caps how much text it will process in a given stretch of time, no matter how much spare computing power sits idle elsewhere.
So the exact same backlog of text can be limited by raw computing power in one setup, and limited by that service's own allowance in the other.
Deleting the source document can't stop there.
Its vector has to go too, marked as gone, or search keeps happily returning something that was supposed to have disappeared.
That's not tidying up after the fact. That's the actual definition of deleting something correctly.
Switching which model produces the vectors is a bigger deal than it first sounds.
Two different models, pointed at the exact same piece of text, land on two vectors that simply don't live in the same space as each other.
So there's no honest way to compare one model's output against the other's, and that single fact shapes everything about how a switch has to happen.
Given that, here's how the switch actually gets made without anything breaking.
The old model keeps answering every single search that comes in, uninterrupted, while a complete second collection gets built from scratch using the new model.
Only once that second collection is entirely finished does anything get pointed toward it. Nothing switches over early, and nothing goes unanswered in between.
Pulling the whole thing together now.

Read a published study for its approach, never for a number lifted out of context. Fingerprint small chunks so an edit only redoes what actually changed. Mark a deletion as gone everywhere, not just at the source. And never point queries at a replacement collection until it's completely ready.
A team currently paying an outside service by the token decides to run the very same model on hardware they own instead.

Out of everything covered here, fingerprinting changed chunks, marking deletions as gone, and building a second collection before switching to it, which of those actually has to change because of that move?
answer: None of those three actually care which kind of ceiling happens to be limiting things at any given moment.
The only thing that genuinely changes is which ceiling applies at all: owned hardware gets limited by its own raw computing power instead of by someone else's allowance.
